ImageDescription.value:
Stairs to Officers’ Row Garden, Alcatraz Island, San Francisco, California, USA
Alcatraz, the rocky island in San Francisco Bay, transformed from a strategic military base to the most notorious maximum security prison in the United States. Originally designated as a military fort to secure the gold rush town in 1850, it later housed the army’s first military prison. Due to its isolated location and treacherous, freezing currents, the Department of Justice took over the island in 1934 and turned it into a federal prison.
Here, under the strictest regime, serious criminals such as Al Capone and “Birdman” Robert Stroud were interned. The concept was simple: anyone who broke the rules ended up in Alcatraz – a place without privileges. Despite 14 escape attempts, the prison is officially considered escape-proof, even if the spectacular escape of 1962 still leaves questions unanswered today. In 1963, operations were discontinued due to high maintenance costs. Another important chapter in the prison’s history is its occupation by activists from the “Indians of All Tribes” (1969–1971), who used the island as a symbol for indigenous rights. Today, Alcatraz is part of the National Recreation Area and attracts millions of visitors annually as a museum.
